# The institutional impossibility of guild socialism 

Geoffrey M Hodgson

 Geoffrey M Hodgson 

Loughborough University London

## Abstract

Guild socialism was developed in the 1906–25 period. It has been held up as a ‘libertarian’ and ‘democratic’ alternative to the statist socialism of the Fabians and the Soviet bloc. This article outlines the basic features of guild socialism, particularly in the most influential version of G. D. H. Cole. Guild socialists wanted to minimise markets and to give higher administrative bodies the right to impose prices in cases of dispute. It is argued here that, despite the intentions of its proponents, guild socialism has a strong centralising dynamic that would undermine its defining aspirations for ‘workers' control’. This centralising dynamic will remain, as long as the guilds are denied legal autonomy, (cooperative) ownership of their means of production and their general right to negotiate prices of their outputs and inputs with buyers and sellers. This diminished capacity for local adjustment, with a potential upward referral of crucial decisions and powers, would add to the informational and task burdens of higher administrative bodies. Much of the previous literature on guild socialism has overlooked these problems. Attention must be paid to legal, as well as other, power relations in the analysis of actual or proposed economic systems.

## 1. The influence and importance of guild socialism

Just over a hundred years ago, guild socialism was at the zenith of its influence. Today, it is sometimes mentioned as an example of decentralised, democratic socialism. But it is rarely examined more closely. Its practical feasibility is simply assumed. If guild socialism is not feasible, then the democratic socialist options are markedly diminished.

Guild socialism emerged in 1906 with Arthur J. Penty’s book on The Restoration of the Gild System (1906). The ‘gild’ description came from a desire to emulate the spirit of craftmanship found in medieval guilds. After Penty’s nostalgic medieval revivalism, other writers adapted the guild idea to modern circumstances. Alfred R. Orage, Samuel G. Hobson, G. D. H. Cole and others founded the National Guilds League in 1915. A core idea was to build upon trade union organisation and promote a strategy of ‘workers’ control’ of industry. 1 

Cole and others were inspired by the writings of William Morris, who celebrated fulfilment through creative work. Syndicalism was another stimulant. Guild socialism also saw itself as a ‘socialist pluralism’ that shifted power away from the central state toward self-governing associations (Laski, 1917; Cole, 1919; Eisfeld, 1996; Runciman, 1997).

For the guild socialists, the worker, rather than the state, was the locus of human emancipation. Socialism would be instigated primarily from below, by organised labour, rather than from above by a political party or a revolutionary vanguard. The system of ‘wage slavery’ would be abolished, leading to ‘workers’ control’ of production. Guild socialism was seen as a ‘democratic’ and ‘libertarian’ alternative to statist socialism and to insurrectionary Marxism. But the guild utopia still envisaged the public ownership of the major industries (Wright, 1979; Stears, 1998).

During the First World War, guild socialism became influential in the trade union movement. Cole became its intellectual leader and his ideas spread in Britain and elsewhere. But following the labour scarcity of the war years, the deep recession of 1920–21 created mass unemployment. Organised labour was then in no position to pursue the guild socialist strategy of ‘encroaching control’. A second reason for the collapse of the movement was the formation in 1920 of the Communist Party of Great Britain (CPGB), promoting the revolutionary overturn of capitalism and allegiance to the infant Bolshevik regime in Russia. This divided the guild socialist movement, with several of its members joining the CPGB in the early 1920s (Cole, 1971, pp. 120–8). The National Guilds League was dissolved in 1925.

Despite its short life, the ideas of the guild socialist movement proved resilient and influential. John Dewey and Bertrand Russell were two of the greatest philosophers of the twentieth century. They were both enduring devotees of guild socialism (Russell, 1918, pp. xi, 13, 80–84; Ryan, 1988, pp. 88–89, 1995, p. 116; Westbrook, 1991, pp. 249, 455–7). Others influenced by guild socialism in its heyday included the future Prime Minister Clement Attlee (Wright, 1979, p. 107), the future leader of the Labour Party George Lansbury (Glass, 1966, p. 39), the economist Lionel Robbins (1971, pp. 56–8, 64–7) – who quickly became a critic – and the prominent socialist academics Harold Laski (Eisfeld, 1996; Lamb, 1999) and Richard H. Tawney (Carpenter, 1922, pp. 97–8; Cole, 1971, p. 128; Wright, 1979, p. 72). Others caught by its spell included Major Clifford H. Douglas, the pioneer of the social credit movement (Hutchinson and Burkitt, 1997), Kingsley Martin, the future editor of the New Statesman, and Victor Gollancz, the publisher (Wright, 1979, pp. 91, 100).

The Independent Labour Party (ILP) adopted a new constitution in 1922, with a strong infusion of guild socialist ideas. Oswald Mosely was initially attracted to guild socialism through the ILP. There are similarities between Cole’s installation of trade unions as part of the planning machinery, and the fascist and corporatist ideas of Mosley and Mussolini, where trade unions are woven into the fabric of the national state. Cole was initially sympathetic to Mussolini’s corporatism, but he quickly recoiled from that misjudgement (Foote, 1997, pp. 120–1, 170).

Others influenced by guild socialism included the Marxist Otto Bauer, who was briefly a minister in the Austrian government (Wright, 1979, p. 108). Bauer popularised Cole’s guild ideas in a number of articles in German (Dale, 2014). Jacob Marschak, the famous mainstream economist and pioneer of econometrics, was a devotee of guild socialism while living in Germany (Hoff, 1981 [1938], pp. 244–5). When he was in Vienna, Karl Polanyi was influenced by Bauer and Marschak. Polanyi became a supporter of guild socialism and introduced its ideas to the Hungarian émigré community in Vienna (Dale, 2014). He elaborated on Cole’s guild socialist ideas in an article in 1922 (Bockman et al., 2016). 2 When Polanyi fled to the UK in 1933, he and Cole became friends (Dale, 2010, pp. 24–31; 2016).

Guild socialism had a lasting impact on Fabianism and the Labour Party. Sidney and Beatrice Webb drafted Clause Four of the UK Labour Party rules, which was adopted in 1918. The text refers to ‘the common ownership of the means of production, distribution and exchange’ under ‘the best obtainable system of popular administration and control’. Of course, the notion of common ownership derives from Robert Owen, Karl Marx and others. But the inclusion of ‘control’ in the 1918 Clause Four has been attributed to the influence of guild socialists. The Webbs (1920) rejected the guild socialist idea of industrial representation, but ‘they drastically modified earlier Fabian proposals in order to provide a measure of worker-control in industry’ (Dahl, 1947, p. 881). In 1923 the ILP’s New Leader newspaper compared the Labour MP Philip Snowden’s motion to the UK Parliament, which proposed the abolition of capitalism and its replacement by ‘public ownership and democratic control of the means of production and distribution’, with an earlier motion in favour of socialism proposed by Keir Hardie at the turn of the century. It noted the inspiration of guild socialism in Snowden’s later motion, with its addition of the words ‘democratic control’ (Wright, 1979, pp. 107–8).

The Hungarian Revolution of 1956 triggered numerous defections from Communist Parties. The democratic aspirations of the emerging New Left bore guild socialist hallmarks. Sedgwick (1961) – who had left the CPGB in 1956 – praised Cole in the New Left Review, admitting that ‘we have caught up with him, about fifty years late.’ In the USA, Dewey fused guild socialism with his radical philosophy of widespread democratic participation. This too became a major influence on the New Left in the 1960s and 1970s (Westbrook, 1991, p. 549).

The phraseology of ‘public ownership under democratic control’ has been repeated since, including by the US socialist politician Bernie Sanders, and by Jeremy Corbyn, the leader of the UK Labour Party from 2015 to 2020. Academics such as Hirst (1994) have embraced much of Cole’s guild socialism. The US economist Hahnel (2005, p. 187) reported that in the 1970s he and Michael Albert had concluded that ‘the visions of a self-managed economy’ shared by guild socialists and others were ‘essentially sound’ but lacked adequate detail on how their alternative to capitalism would work. Before he became a Labour MP, Wright (1979) delved into guild socialism. In his plea for ‘libertarian socialism’, the former member of the Labour government (and now Lord) Hain (2015, pp. 143–5) cited guild socialism as a major inspiration.

When Corbyn was Labour leader, brief mentions of guild socialism cropped up in discussions of Labour Party policy, proposing it as a decentralised and non-bureaucratic model for the future (Gowan, 2018; Wainwright, 2018; Beckett, 2019). In his introduction to his edited book on socialist economic policy, McDonnell (2018, p. x), then Deputy Leader of the Labour Party, addressed ‘everything from Marxism to G. D. H. Cole and the guild socialists’, seemingly implying that there is a substantial political distance between the two. 3 In their essay in McDonnell’s volume, Guinan and Hanna (2018, pp. 114–15) endorsed Cole’s wide promotion of economic democracy. On the same page, they began to discuss the Mondragon worker cooperatives in Spain, noting their ‘highly egalitarian and cooperative internal culture.’

But Guinan and Hanna failed to note that Cole (1920B, pp. 58–59; 192–204) opposed worker cooperatives in the production sector, where, by definition, the workers themselves would own most shares in the enterprise. Accordingly, Cole was critical of the building ‘guilds’ that were set up to help deal with the housing shortage after the First World War. Cole objected that they would be a form of cooperative production, exposed to capitalist market forces. Cole wrote: ‘Building Guilds are not Guild Socialism’ (Carpenter, 1973, pp. 102–3). Cole was generally critical of producer cooperatives. He never promoted worker cooperatives, except in the distribution and press sectors. 4 

Cole’s writings on guild socialism are periodically cited as exemplars of decentralised socialism. But his works are rarely probed in detail, and some mischaracterisations persist. 5 If guild socialism is to be more than a vague slogan for some kind of devolved socialism, then it has to be examined much more closely, and evaluated in the light of insights from modern social science.

## 2. Some key issues

A rival decentralised option, which unlike guild socialism has been tested in practice in Mondragon and elsewhere, involves legally autonomous worker cooperatives, which are owned by their workers. As legally constituted entities, they trade on markets. But many socialists
